newsitem.title: USA: Rocky trade seen on Wall St ahead of Q2 earnings.
newsitem.headline: Rocky trade seen on Wall St ahead of Q2 earnings.

text.p: Wall Street's whiplash this week is a sign stocks could be at their near-term peaks, ushering in a period of volatile trading as investors brace for the onslaught of quarterly corporate earnings reports.
The trading spikes Monday and Tuesday reflect increasing jitters among investors following the Dow industrials rally of over 21 percent since mid-April, market analysts said.
Nerves will be further tested by any signs of a slowdown in corporate profits in the coming weeks.
"The market is up so much...that anything that is anyway out of line will be punished really drastically," said Charles Pradilla, market analyst at Cowen and Co.
Strong first quarter corporate profits triggered the latest rally beginning in mid-April, which came after a near 10 percent Dow pullback.
But as Wall Street heads into the end of the second quarter on Monday, blue chips stocks are near all-time highs.
"Now the room for disappointments is very thin," said Bruce Bittles, market strategist at J.C. Bradford.
In a fresh episode of volatility, the Dow was off about 90 points at 7667 on Wednesday afternoon, after hitting a session high of 7812. It closed at a record high 7796.51 on Friday.
On Monday the Dow sank 192 points in a late-day selloff triggered by remarks from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on the possible Japanese sale of U.S. Treasuries.
On Tuesday the blue-chip gauge rocketed back 154 points as buyers rushed in after Japanese officials backtracked softening Hashimoto's remarks and claiming they had been misinterpreted.

"That's what a bull market does," said Jonathan Dodd, technical analyst at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. "It can have sharp reactions but those reactions are usually short-lived, no matter what the reason."
Analysts said they expected investors to reactly sharply - particularly in the negative direction - during the earnings period if earnings warrant.

Wall Street analysts are expecting the Standard and Poor's 500 companies to report a an average of a 9.2 percent rise in second quarter operating profits, according to First Call. This comes after a 15.1 percent rise in first quarter earnings.

Operating profits forecasts appear on the surface to indicate an earnings slowdown, but the first quarter gains were exaggerated due to 1996's weak earnings which were hurt by severe weather and other factors.

Analysts are typically conservative in their estimates heading into the quarterly earnings period, which would indicate a second quarter S&P 500 earnings rise of about 12 percent, said Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call.
"The slowdown, despite the raw numbers, isn't going to be starting in the second quarter," Hill said. "But the raw numbers may panic some people into thinking it's starting."
Because stocks have rallied ahead of the earnings period, even companies that meet or beat analysts' profit forecasts may not see their shares benefit.

"It's our opinion that at these levels we're more likely to see the market take a negative view of anything that is not well above expectations," said Robert Walberg, chief equity analyst at Briefing.Com.
"That sets us up for a bit of a correction here."
He said the Dow could pull back to the 7100-7000 level in the correction.
